newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FORECAST - WIFO sees mild 1997 Austria growth pickup.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - WIFO sees mild 1997 Austria growth pickup.

text.p: Austria's economic research institute WIFO raised its growth forecast for the Austrian economy next year, based on expectations of strong exports and investment, and predicted an acceleration of growth in 1998.
WIFO, whose figures form the basis of government policy, revised its 1997 gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecast upward to 1.2 percent from 1.0 and its 1996 estimate to 0.8 percent from 0.7.
It forecast GDP growth would reach 2.2 percent in 1998.
"The economy will only see a slight pick-up in 1997, but at a first glance 1998 offers cause for cautious optimism," the institute said in a statement released ahead of a news conference.

Real growth remained below the European average of 2.0 percent, due in part to slow demand by Austria's main trading partners, Germany, Italy and Switzerland, it noted. A strict fiscal policy and continuing crisis in the tourism industry were further factors affecting economic growth.
"The growth difference among European industrial nations, particularly Germany, should even out in 1998," WIFO added.

The Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday also raised its 1996 forecast for Austrian economic growth to 1.1 percent from 0.8 percent in June. It predicts GDP growth of 1.4 percent for 1997.

WIFO saw foreign demand boosted by improved competitivity resulting from greater currency stability in preparation for European Monetary Union (EMU), strong growth of industrial productivity and restrained wage policies.
However, domestic demand was expected to remain weak in 1997, primarily due to the government's stringent budgetary measures ahead of EMU and an unfavourable job market climate.
WIFO upped its current account deficit forecast for 1997 to 44 billion schillings from 25.8 billion and for 1996 to 47 billion schillings from its previous estimate of 44.4 billion.
"The high current account deficit threatens to become a major economic problem," WIFO said.
Inflation was seen at 1.9 percent for 1997, a slight rise from previous estimates of 1.7, buoyed by a rise in crude oil prices, and only expected to fall in 1998 to 1.6 percent.
